questions.stem: What is the difference between 「食べます」 and 「食べる」?
options: Same meaning; the first is past, the second present
The first is a question, the second a statement
The first is spoken; the second is only written
Same meaning; the first is polite, the second plain
questions.explanation: Both mean 'eat'. 「食べます」 is the polite ます form used with teachers, strangers and in class; 「食べる」 is the plain form used with friends and family. Neither is past tense.

questions.stem: Who would you normally speak to in plain form, such as 「行く？」?
options: Your friend's grandmother
A teacher you have just met
A shop assistant who is serving you
A close friend of your own age
questions.explanation: Plain form signals closeness, so it suits friends and family. With older people, teachers and strangers, the polite です/ます form is the safe choice.

questions.stem: A student asks a teacher 「先生、あした、テストある？」. What is wrong with it?
options: It uses plain form where polite form is expected
It uses the wrong particle after the word for tomorrow
It should begin with the teacher's family name
It is a statement, so it cannot be a question
questions.explanation: The grammar is fine between friends, but a teacher should hear 「先生、あした、テストがありますか。」 Register, not grammar, is the mistake here.

questions.stem: In Japanese, what mainly decides the choice between 「行く」 and 「行きます」?
options: Whether the speaker is male or female
Whether the place being talked about is near or far
Your relationship with the listener and the setting
Whether the action is in the past or the future
questions.explanation: Both are non-past forms of 'go'. Which one you use depends on who you are talking to and where, which is why Japanese speakers are constantly judging relationships as they talk.

questions.stem: Which word for 'I' suits almost any situation, including formal ones?
options: 私
ぼく
おれ
あたし
questions.explanation: 「私」 (わたし) is neutral and polite. 「ぼく」 is used mainly by boys and men, 「おれ」 is casual and mainly male, and 「あたし」 is casual and mainly female.

questions.stem: Which word for 'I' is casual and used mostly by men and boys among friends?
options: あなた
おれ
私
わたくし
questions.explanation: 「おれ」 is casual and would sound rough in a job interview. 「わたくし」 is the most formal 'I', and 「あなた」 means 'you', not 'I'.

questions.stem: Some speakers use 「じぶん」 ('oneself') as their word for 'I'. What does this show?
options: Japanese has only a single word for 'I', which everyone has to use
First-person words in Japanese are fixed by a government list
Only young children are allowed to choose a word for 'I'
Speakers choose a word for 'I' that fits how they see themselves
questions.explanation: Japanese has several words for 'I', each carrying a different image. Some speakers, including some non-binary people, choose 「じぶん」 because it feels less tied to gender than 「ぼく」 or 「あたし」 - identity shaping language.

questions.stem: What is 「けいご」?
options: A regional dialect spoken in western Japan
The casual slang used by teenagers
The language used only in old poetry
Respectful language used to show politeness
questions.explanation: 「けいご」 covers the special verbs and forms used to show respect, heard in shops, business and formal speech. Students meet it first in set phrases such as 「いらっしゃいませ」.

questions.stem: When do you hear 「いらっしゃいませ」?
options: When staff welcome customers into a shop
When a guest leaves someone's home
When friends say goodbye to each other after school
When someone answers the phone at home
questions.explanation: 「いらっしゃいませ」 is the welcome staff call out as customers come into a shop or restaurant. It is built on いらっしゃる, the respectful verb for 'come'.

questions.stem: A shop assistant says 「かしこまりました」. What does it mean?
options: Welcome to our shop
Certainly, I understand
Please come again
Sorry to keep you waiting
questions.explanation: 「かしこまりました」 is the けいご way to say 'understood' when taking an order or request. A friend would just say 「わかった」.

questions.stem: What does 「しょうしょうおまちください」 mean?
options: Please pay over here
Please wait a moment
Please come in
Please take a seat
questions.explanation: 「しょうしょう」 is a formal 'a little', and 「おまちください」 is a respectful 'please wait'. In everyday speech the same request is 「ちょっとまってください」.

questions.stem: 「めしあがる」 is a respectful verb. Which ordinary verb does it replace?
options: 食べる
見せる
行く
言う
questions.explanation: 「めしあがる」 is the respectful verb for eating (and drinking), used of someone you are honouring: 「何をめしあがりますか。」 You never use it about yourself.

questions.stem: What is the difference between respectful and humble language in けいご?
options: Respectful raises the other person; humble lowers yourself
Respectful is spoken; humble is used only in writing
Respectful is for family; humble is for close friends
Respectful is old-fashioned; humble is the modern everyday form
questions.explanation: Both show respect, from opposite directions. 「めしあがる」 lifts the person eating; 「もうします」 lowers the speaker. Together with です/ます they are the main parts of けいご.

questions.stem: Someone introduces themselves with 「スミスともうします」. Why 「もうします」 rather than 「いいます」?
options: It is humble, politely lowering the speaker
It shows that the speaker's name is a foreign one
It is the past tense of 「いいます」
It is the form that children use
questions.explanation: 「もうします」 is the humble verb for 'to be called'. It is heard in formal self-introductions, interviews and on the phone.

questions.stem: What do 「うち」 and 「そと」 mean as a cultural idea?
options: Japanese food and food from overseas
Your own group and those outside it
Only the inside and outside of a house
Indoor and outdoor activities at school
questions.explanation: 「うち」 (inside) is the group you belong to - family, class, workplace - and 「そと」 (outside) is everyone else. The line decides much of the language you choose.

questions.stem: In polite speech to someone outside the family, which pair is correct?
options: お母さん for your own mother and for theirs
母 for your own mother, お母さん for theirs
お母さん for your own mother, 母 for theirs
母 for your own mother and for theirs
questions.explanation: Your family is part of your うち, so to outsiders you use the plain 「母」 (はは). Someone else's mother gets the respectful 「お母さん」. Within the family, お母さん is used to address her.

questions.stem: Talking to your teacher about your own father, which word fits best?
options: お父さま
父さま
父
お父さん
questions.explanation: 「父」 (ちち) is the humble word for your own father when speaking to someone outside the family. 「お父さん」 and 「お父さま」 raise him, which suits someone else's father.

questions.stem: Which suffix is the safe, general choice after someone's name?
options: 〜ちゃん
〜くん
〜さま
〜さん
questions.explanation: 「〜さん」 suits almost anyone. 「〜ちゃん」 is affectionate, for small children and close friends; 「〜さま」 is very formal, for customers.

questions.stem: Why should you never add 〜さん to your own name?
options: It shows respect, so using it on yourself sounds boastful
It is a suffix used only for women and girls
It is a suffix that is only ever used in written Japanese
It is a suffix used only for family members
questions.explanation: Honorific suffixes raise the person named. Introduce yourself as 「スミスです」, never 「スミスさんです」.

questions.stem: Who is addressed with 〜先生?
options: Anyone older than you
Only school principals
Teachers, and also doctors
Only students at university
questions.explanation: 「先生」 is used for teachers and also for doctors and some other professionals. It is used on its own as a form of address, so students call their teacher simply 「先生」.

questions.stem: Why might a teacher use 〜さん for every student, rather than 〜くん for boys?
options: 〜さん suits everyone, so no one is labelled by gender
〜くん is considered a rude word in every possible situation
〜さん is faster to write on the class roll
〜くん can only be used in western Japan
questions.explanation: 「〜くん」 is often used for boys and juniors, but it is not a rule. Using 「〜さん」 for all students treats everyone alike and suits students of any gender.

questions.stem: Where is 〜さま used?
options: For members of your own family
For small children and babies
For customers, and on envelopes
Between close friends at school
questions.explanation: 「〜さま」 is a step above 「〜さん」. It appears in 「おきゃくさま」 (customer), on envelopes, and in the restaurant question 「何名さまですか」.

questions.stem: A friend replies 「その日はちょっと…」 to an invitation. What do they mean?
options: They can come for a short while
They will be a little late
They are a little bit busy but will come
They cannot come, said politely
questions.explanation: Trailing off after 「ちょっと」 is the usual soft refusal. The listener understands 'no' without hearing it, and the friendship is spared a flat refusal.

questions.stem: What are あいづち?
options: Words borrowed from English and written in katakana
The bows people make when meeting someone for the first time
Short responses such as 「はい」 and 「へえ」 that show you are listening
Polite phrases written at the very start of a formal business letter
questions.explanation: あいづち such as 「はい」, 「ええ」, 「そうですか」 and 「なるほど」 are dropped in while someone talks. They keep the conversation going.

questions.stem: A listener keeps saying 「はい、はい」 during a phone call. Does it mean they agree?
options: No, it means they could not hear you
Not necessarily; it shows they are following
Yes, it always means they fully agree
No, it means they would like to end the call soon
questions.explanation: あいづち signal attention, not agreement. Learners who take every 「はい」 as a yes can misread a conversation badly.

questions.stem: Your Japanese is praised: 「日本語がじょうずですね。」 What is the usual modest reply?
options: はい、とてもじょうずです。
はい、そうですね。
ええ、じょうずでしょう。
いいえ、まだまだです。
questions.explanation: Deflecting praise is the expected response. Agreeing that you are skilful, as the other replies do, sounds boastful in Japanese even if it is true.

questions.stem: The value often called わ ('harmony') shows up in language mainly as:
options: Softened refusals and avoiding open disagreement
Loud and direct statements of a person's own opinion
Heavy use of English loanwords in speech
Speaking plain form to everyone you meet
questions.explanation: Softeners such as 「ちょっと」 and 「あまり」, unfinished refusals and deflected praise all keep conflict low. They are habits of the language, not a description of every speaker.

questions.stem: What is おみやげ?
options: A gift, often local food, brought back from a trip
A gift given to a baby on its first birthday
Money given to children at New Year
A thank-you letter written after visiting someone's home
questions.explanation: Bringing おみやげ back for family, classmates or colleagues is a strong custom. Each region and tourist spot has its own speciality sweets to take home.

questions.stem: Why might someone avoid giving a set of four items as a gift?
options: Shops in Japan do not sell items in fours
Gifts must always come in even numbers
「し」, one reading of 四, sounds like 'death'
Four is a lucky number kept for weddings
questions.explanation: 四 can be read 「し」, which sounds like the word for death, so sets of four are traditionally avoided. It is also why 四 is often read 「よん」.

questions.stem: What is おとしだま?
options: Food offered at a shrine in summer
Money given to children at New Year
A box of sweets brought back from a trip
A gift given at the end of the school year
questions.explanation: おとしだま is given to children by parents and relatives during おしょうがつ, the New Year holiday, usually in small decorated envelopes.

questions.stem: How are gifts traditionally given and received in Japan?
options: Wrapped in black-and-white paper
With both hands, often with a slight bow
With the left hand only, palm facing down
Placed on the table without a word
questions.explanation: Using both hands shows care, and the same goes for business cards. Black-and-white wrapping is linked with funerals.

questions.stem: A visitor hands over a gift saying 「ほんのきもちです」. What do they mean?
options: I hope you enjoy eating it
Please open it right now
I bought it in Australia
It's just a small token
questions.explanation: 「ほんのきもちです」 - literally 'it is only my feelings' - plays down the gift, in the same modest spirit as deflecting praise.

questions.stem: What is 花見?
options: Picking flowers for a wedding
Viewing the cherry blossoms in spring
A flower market that is held each summer
Arranging flowers in a vase
questions.explanation: 花見 (はなみ) - 'flower viewing' - means gathering under the cherry blossoms with food and friends. The kanji say exactly that: flower + see.

questions.stem: The word 花火 is made of 'flower' and 'fire'. What does it mean?
options: A bushfire
A red flower
A candle
Fireworks
questions.explanation: 花火 (はなび) are fireworks - flowers of fire - and summer 花火 festivals are a highlight of the season.

questions.stem: When Australia is in summer, what season is it in Japan?
options: Summer
Spring
Autumn
Winter
questions.explanation: Japan is in the northern hemisphere, so its seasons are the reverse of Australia's. Christmas and New Year fall in the Japanese winter.

questions.stem: In which month does the Japanese school year usually begin?
options: January
February
September
April
questions.explanation: The Japanese school year starts in April, in spring, so entrance ceremonies often happen as the cherry blossoms come out. Australian schools start in late January or early February.

questions.stem: What is said to people in late December, before the New Year?
options: おたんじょうび、おめでとう。
いただきます。
よいお年を。
あけましておめでとうございます。
questions.explanation: 「よいお年を」 ('have a good year') is said before the New Year. 「あけましておめでとうございます」 is only said once the New Year has begun.

questions.stem: What is ゴールデンウィーク?
options: A week of school examinations held in the middle of winter
A summer festival famous for its golden fireworks
A week of sales in the shops just before New Year
A cluster of public holidays from late April to early May
questions.explanation: Several public holidays fall close together, so many people travel. The name is itself made-in-Japan English (わせいえいご).

questions.stem: What happens at 七五三?
options: Students celebrate the end of their final exams
Families eat seven, five and three dishes at New Year
Families visit their ancestors' graves in summer
Children aged three, five and seven visit a shrine
questions.explanation: At 七五三 (しちごさん), in November, families take young children, often in traditional dress, to a shrine to celebrate their growth.

questions.stem: What is せいじんしき?
options: A wedding ceremony held at a shrine
A ceremony held for people retiring from work
A ceremony for young people reaching adulthood
A ceremony for children starting primary school
questions.explanation: せいじんしき (coming-of-age ceremonies) are usually held in January. Many participants wear formal kimono. Starting school is marked by a different ceremony, the にゅうがくしき.

questions.stem: What does かんさいべん refer to?
options: The traditional language of Okinawa
The standard Japanese heard on the TV news
The dialect of the Osaka and Kyoto region
The dialect spoken across Hokkaido
questions.explanation: かんさいべん is the best-known dialect of Japanese, heard in Osaka, Kyoto and nearby. It is famous from comedy and television.

questions.stem: In かんさいべん, what does 「おおきに」 mean?
options: Thank you
Very big
Goodbye
Excuse me
questions.explanation: 「おおきに」 means 'thank you'. It began as 'greatly', short for 「おおきにありがとう」, so it looks like 「おおきい」 (big), but on its own in the dialect it is a word of thanks.

questions.stem: In かんさいべん, what does 「あかん」 mean?
options: No good, not allowed
Red
Delicious
Let's go
questions.explanation: 「あかん」 is the かんさいべん equivalent of 「だめ」. It has nothing to do with 「あかい」 (red), despite the sound.

questions.stem: What does 「めっちゃ」 mean, a word from western Japan now used widely?
options: Never
A little
Messy
Very
questions.explanation: 「めっちゃ」 means 'very' and works like 「とても」 in casual speech: 「めっちゃおいしい」. It began in western Japan and spread among young people everywhere.

questions.stem: In かんさいべん, 「わからへん」 means the same as which standard form?
options: わかります
わからない
わかった
わかる
questions.explanation: かんさいべん often makes the negative with 「〜へん」 where standard Japanese uses 「〜ない」, so 「わからへん」 is 'I don't understand'.

questions.stem: Why do national newsreaders use standard Japanese rather than a regional dialect?
options: Regional dialects have no way of being written
It is the oldest of all the Japanese dialects
It is understood everywhere and heard as neutral
Regional dialects are banned from all broadcasts
questions.explanation: Standard Japanese is based on the speech of the とうきょう area and is taught in every school. Many speakers use it at work or on air and their own dialect at home - a choice that says something about identity.

questions.stem: What is アイヌ語?
options: A sign language used in Japanese schools
The language of the Ainu, an Indigenous people of northern Japan
A dialect of standard Japanese spoken in the far south of Japan
An old form of Japanese found only in poetry
questions.explanation: アイヌ語 is the language of the Ainu, who are recognised as an Indigenous people of Japan. Their homeland includes Hokkaido.

questions.stem: How is アイヌ語 related to Japanese?
options: It is a mixture of Japanese and Russian
It is a separate language, not a dialect of Japanese
It is the oldest surviving form of the Japanese language
It is Japanese written entirely in katakana
questions.explanation: アイヌ語 has its own grammar and vocabulary and is not related to Japanese. Linguists class it as an isolate - a language with no known relatives.

questions.stem: Many place names in which part of Japan come from アイヌ語?
options: Okinawa
Shikoku
The Kansai region
Hokkaido
questions.explanation: Hokkaido is part of the Ainu homeland, and many of its place names come from アイヌ語 words, later written with kanji or kana.

questions.stem: What is the situation of アイヌ語 today?
options: It is the main language taught in all Hokkaido schools
It is spoken at home by most people in Hokkaido
It has disappeared, leaving no records behind
It is endangered, and there are efforts to revive it
questions.explanation: UNESCO lists アイヌ語 as critically endangered. Classes, museums, songs and recordings keep it alive and help new learners.

questions.stem: What are the Ryukyuan languages?
options: Languages brought to Japan from China by traders
Another name for the languages of the Ainu people
Languages of Okinawa and nearby islands, related to Japanese
Dialects of Japanese spoken across the northern island of Hokkaido
questions.explanation: The Ryukyuan languages, such as Okinawan, are spoken in the island chain south of Kyushu. They share an ancestor with Japanese.

questions.stem: In Okinawa, what does 「めんそーれ」 mean?
options: Goodbye
Delicious
Welcome
Thank you
questions.explanation: 「めんそーれ」 is the Okinawan word of welcome, often seen on signs greeting visitors to Okinawa. It does the job of 「いらっしゃいませ」.

questions.stem: Why are the Ryukyuan languages counted as languages rather than dialects of Japanese?
options: They are used only in writing and have no spoken form
They are related, but neither side can understand the other
They are written in an alphabet unlike anything used in Japan
They have no connection at all with the Japanese language
questions.explanation: Okinawan and standard Japanese come from a common ancestor but are not mutually understandable, much as English and German are related but separate. Several Ryukyuan languages are endangered.

questions.stem: Japanese divers worked in which industry from the late 1800s, especially around Broome?
options: Wheat farming
Cattle droving
Pearling
Wool shearing
questions.explanation: Japanese divers were central to the pearling industry in Broome and Thursday Island. Broome's Japanese cemetery is a reminder of how dangerous the work was.

questions.stem: What is a sister-city link, like those between many Australian and Japanese towns?
options: A sports league that two cities play in together
A formal friendship for exchanges between two cities
A trade treaty signed between two national governments
A pair of cities that happen to share the same name
questions.explanation: Sister cities organise school exchanges, visits and cultural events. Many Australian towns and cities have a Japanese sister city.

questions.stem: When you give an Acknowledgement of Country in Japanese, what do you name?
options: The part of Japan your teacher comes from
The Traditional Owners of the land where you are
The Japanese sister city your school is linked with
The first Japanese person to visit Australia
questions.explanation: An Acknowledgement of Country names the local Country and its Traditional Owners, whatever the language. Saying it in Japanese introduces Australia's First Peoples to a Japanese-speaking audience.

questions.stem: Where do you take your shoes off when entering a Japanese home?
options: Just inside the living room door
At the front gate of the garden
Beside the kitchen table
At the げんかん, the entrance area
questions.explanation: The げんかん is a step down at the entrance where shoes are left, usually turned to face the door. Slippers are often worn inside.

questions.stem: Why is it poor manners to stand chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice?
options: It shows you have finished eating
It means the rice is too hot
It recalls rice offered at funerals
It means you would like more rice
questions.explanation: Chopsticks standing in rice are associated with offerings to the dead, so it is avoided at the table. Passing food from chopstick to chopstick is avoided for a similar reason.

questions.stem: What are 外来語?
options: Words used only in the Kansai region
The names of foreign countries only
Loanwords, mostly written in katakana
Words made up of exactly two kanji
questions.explanation: 外来語 (がいらいご) - literally 'words that came from outside' - are loanwords such as 「テレビ」 and 「パン」. Most are written in katakana.

questions.stem: What does サラリーマン mean in Japanese?
options: A salary paid each month
A manager in a shop
An office worker on a salary
A man who sells salads at a market
questions.explanation: サラリーマン is made in Japan from 'salary' and 'man' - わせいえいご. An English speaker would say 'office worker'.

questions.stem: What does パソコン mean?
options: A personal computer
A passport photo
A password
A parcel delivery
questions.explanation: パソコン is a shortened form of 「パーソナル・コンピューター」. Japanese often clips long loanwords to four syllables or so.

questions.stem: In Japanese, what is a コンセント?
options: A music concert
A plan or concept
A power point in the wall
Permission to do something
questions.explanation: コンセント is わせいえいご for a power point, not 'consent'. A false friend like this can confuse both learners and visitors.

questions.stem: What is わせいえいご?
options: English words used just as in English
Japanese words borrowed into English
The English taught in Japanese schools
Words made in Japan from English parts
questions.explanation: わせいえいご ('Japan-made English') includes サラリーマン and コンセント. They look English, but an English speaker may not understand them.

questions.stem: Which word came into Japanese from Portuguese, not English?
options: テレビ
バス
ケーキ
パン
questions.explanation: パン (bread) comes from Portuguese 'pão', borrowed when Portuguese traders reached Japan in the 1500s, long before most English loanwords.

questions.stem: From which language does アルバイト ('part-time job') come?
options: German
English
French
Portuguese
questions.explanation: アルバイト comes from German 'Arbeit' (work). In Japanese it means a part-time job, often shortened to 「バイト」.

questions.stem: What does マナーモード mean on a Japanese phone?
options: Flight mode
Driving mode
Silent mode
Battery-saving mode
questions.explanation: マナーモード - 'manner mode' - is the setting for being polite in public, as on trains. The phrase is わせいえいご.

questions.stem: What are おんよみ readings of kanji?
options: Readings native to the Japanese language
Readings used only for people's names
Readings used only in the Kansai dialect
Readings based on old Chinese pronunciation
questions.explanation: おんよみ came to Japan with the characters themselves and imitate how they were said in Chinese. 学 read がく and 校 read こう are おんよみ.

questions.stem: What are くんよみ readings of kanji?
options: Readings borrowed from the old Chinese pronunciation
Readings used only inside compound words
Readings used only for writing numbers
Native Japanese words matched to a kanji's meaning
questions.explanation: くんよみ are Japanese words given to a kanji with the same meaning, so 山 is read やま and 川 かわ when they stand alone.

questions.stem: On its own, 山 is read やま. In 火山 it is read ざん. Which statement is right?
options: やま is the くんよみ; ざん comes from the おんよみ
やま is the おんよみ; ざん comes from the くんよみ
やま and ざん are both くんよみ readings
やま and ざん are both おんよみ readings
questions.explanation: やま is the native word, so it is the くんよみ. さん is the おんよみ, and in 火山 (かざん, volcano) the さ sound changes to ざ after another kanji.

questions.stem: How is 人 read when it stands alone, as in 「あの人」?
options: ひと
じん
にん
り
questions.explanation: On its own, 人 takes its くんよみ, ひと. The おんよみ じん and にん appear in compounds.

questions.stem: How is 人 read in 日本人?
options: ひと
にん
り
じん
questions.explanation: After a country, 人 is read じん: 日本人 (にほんじん), オーストラリア人. にん is the reading used when counting, as in 三人.

questions.stem: How is 人 read in 三人?
options: じん
ひと
り
にん
questions.explanation: 三人 is さんにん. Counting from three people up uses にん, but one and two people are irregular: 一人 (ひとり) and 二人 (ふたり).

questions.stem: In 日曜日, how are the two 日 read, in order?
options: び, then にち
にち, then にち
にち, then び
ひ, then にち
questions.explanation: 日曜日 is にちようび. The first 日 is the おんよみ にち; the second is the くんよみ ひ, which softens to び after another kanji.

questions.stem: How is 日 read in 日本?
options: にち
ひ
か
に
questions.explanation: 日本 is にほん (also にっぽん). 日 has an unusually large number of readings: 毎日 (まいにち), 日曜日 (にちようび), and even 今日 (きょう), where the two kanji are read together.

questions.stem: How is 生 read in 先生, and in 生きる?
options: せい, then なま
せい, then い
い, then せい
しょう, then う
questions.explanation: 先生 is せんせい, with the おんよみ せい. In 生きる (いきる, to live) the くんよみ い is followed by おくりがな.

questions.stem: Why can one kanji have several readings, as 日 does in 日本, 毎日 and 日曜日?
options: Chinese readings were borrowed alongside the native word
Each region of Japan reads the same kanji in its own way
The readings were changed in a later spelling reform
Each reading gives the kanji a completely new meaning
questions.explanation: When kanji came to Japan, they kept Chinese-based readings (おんよみ) and were also given the Japanese word with the same meaning (くんよみ). Most common kanji therefore have both.

questions.stem: What is おくりがな?
options: Small kana written above kanji to show the reading
Katakana used for words from other languages
A numbered list of the strokes in a kanji
Hiragana written after a kanji to complete a word
questions.explanation: In 食べる, the べる is おくりがな: it carries the changing ending while the kanji carries the meaning. Small reading aids above kanji are ふりがな.

questions.stem: In 食べる, which part is the おくりがな?
options: べる
食
る
食べ
questions.explanation: Everything after the kanji is おくりがな: 食 + べる. When the verb changes, the おくりがな changes and the kanji stays: 食べます, 食べて.

questions.stem: Which is written correctly with kanji and おくりがな?
options: 新らしい
新たらしい
新しい
新い
questions.explanation: あたらしい is written 新しい: the kanji covers あたら, and しい is the おくりがな. 「新らしい」 is a common learner error.

questions.stem: Kanji with 亻 on the left, such as 休 and 体, often relate to what?
options: People
Water
Trees
Speech
questions.explanation: 亻 is a squeezed form of 人. 休 (rest) is a person beside a tree, and 体 (body) is about people too.

questions.stem: The radical 氵 is a squeezed form of which kanji?
options: 火
木
川
水
questions.explanation: 氵 is the water radical, a compressed 水. Kanji with it on the left usually have to do with water, such as seas, rivers and swimming.

questions.stem: 語, 読 and 話 share the radical 言. What area of meaning do they share?
options: Time and days
People and families
Words and speaking
Eating and drinking
questions.explanation: 言 means 'say', and kanji built on it are about language: 語 (language), 読 (read), 話 (speak).

questions.stem: Which kanji has 木 (tree) as its left-hand part?
options: 校
休
体
何
questions.explanation: 校 (school) has 木 on the left. 休 also contains 木, but on the right, next to the person radical 亻.

questions.stem: If 小学校 is primary school, what is 中学校?
options: Junior high school
University
Kindergarten
Senior high school
questions.explanation: 小 is small and 中 is middle, so 中学校 (ちゅうがっこう) is the middle school - junior high. Senior high school is 高校 (こうこう), with 高 for high.

questions.stem: If 電 means electricity and 車 means vehicle, what is 電車?
options: A train
A car
A bicycle
A plane
questions.explanation: 電車 (でんしゃ) is an electric vehicle - a train. 車 on its own (くるま) is a car.

questions.stem: 今週 means 'this week'. What does 来週 mean?
options: Last week
Every week
This weekend
Next week
questions.explanation: 来 means 'come', so 来週 (らいしゅう) is the coming week. Last week is 先週 and every week 毎週.

questions.stem: What does 入口 mean, built from 'enter' and 'mouth'?
options: Waiting room
Entrance
Exit
Ticket gate
questions.explanation: 口 here means an opening. 入口 (いりぐち) is the way in, and 出口 (でぐち), with 出 for 'go out', is the exit.

questions.stem: Using what you know of 白 and 黒, what is a 白黒 photo?
options: Faded with age
Taken at night
Black and white
Brightly coloured
questions.explanation: 白 is white and 黒 is black, so 白黒 (しろくろ) is black and white. Japanese puts white first where English puts black first.

questions.stem: What is the general rule for stroke order in kanji?
options: The outside strokes are always last
The longest stroke always comes first
Top to bottom, and left to right
Bottom to top, and right to left
questions.explanation: Most kanji are written from top to bottom and from left to right. Further rules settle the cases those two do not.

questions.stem: When a horizontal and a vertical stroke cross, as in 十, which is usually written first?
options: Whichever stroke is shorter
The horizontal stroke
The vertical stroke
Whichever stroke is longer
questions.explanation: 十 is written horizontal first, then vertical. The same order applies in many kanji with a crossing, such as 木.

questions.stem: In 中, when is the long vertical stroke written?
options: Third
Last
First
Second
questions.explanation: A vertical stroke that runs right through a kanji is written last, after the box it cuts through.

questions.stem: Which stroke-order rule does 小 show?
options: From right to left across the kanji
From the bottom of the kanji upwards
The centre first, then the two sides
The two sides first, then the centre
questions.explanation: When a kanji is symmetrical around a central stroke, as 小 is, the centre is written first and then the left and right.

questions.stem: In 国, when is the bottom stroke of the outer frame written?
options: Last, after the inside is filled in
First, before any other stroke
Straight after the left side
After the top side, but before the inside
questions.explanation: In an enclosed kanji, you write the frame's left, top and right sides, fill in the inside, and close the box with the bottom stroke last.

questions.stem: 右 and 左 look alike. How does their first stroke differ?
options: 右 starts with the slanting stroke; 左 with the horizontal
右 starts with the horizontal; 左 with the slanting stroke
Both start with the horizontal stroke
Both start with the slanting stroke
questions.explanation: In 右 the short slanting stroke comes first, then the horizontal. In 左 the horizontal comes first. It is a well-known exception worth learning.

questions.stem: What is げんこうようし?
options: Lined paper with wide gaps for writing English letters
Thin paper used only for brush calligraphy
A printed form for writing school reports
Squared paper for Japanese, one character per square
questions.explanation: Each kana, kanji and punctuation mark gets its own square. Students use it for compositions, and it makes length easy to count.

questions.stem: How is vertical writing on げんこうようし read?
options: Top to bottom, columns from right to left
Top to bottom, columns from left to right
Left to right, lines from top to bottom
Bottom to top, columns from right to left
questions.explanation: Vertical Japanese starts at the top right of the page and moves left column by column. Books written this way open from what English readers think of as the back.

questions.stem: On げんこうようし, how do you start a new paragraph?
options: Draw a small circle in the first square
Leave three squares blank
Leave the first square blank
Leave a whole column blank
questions.explanation: A new paragraph begins one square in. Blank columns are used around the title and name, not between paragraphs.

questions.stem: How do small kana such as ゃ and っ go on げんこうようし?
options: They are left out altogether
Each takes its own square
They share the square before them
They are written above the squares
questions.explanation: Small kana take a full square of their own, written small and towards the top right of the square in vertical writing.

questions.stem: Where does 。 usually go on げんこうようし?
options: Nowhere; squared paper has no punctuation
In its own square, like a character
In the same square as the next character
Only at the end of each paragraph
questions.explanation: Punctuation marks take a square each, sitting in the top right corner of the square in vertical writing.

questions.stem: On vertical げんこうようし, a 。 would fall at the top of a new column. What do you do?
options: Leave that whole column blank instead
Leave the 。 out of the sentence altogether
Put it in the last square of the column before
Write it at the top of the new column as usual
questions.explanation: A column should not begin with a punctuation mark, so the 。 shares the last square with the final character, or sits just below the grid.
